_about: AirDriver chipset database. Maps USB/PCI VID:PID -> chipset -> driver install strategy. 'usb_ids' are lowercase 'vid:pid' (works for PCI ids too). 'kernel_native' tells AirDriver when an in-kernel driver already exists so it can SKIP a pointless DKMS build. 'drivers' are tried in 'priority' order (1 = first). 'monitor_mode'/'injection' are honest capability flags for pentest use; some chips connect fine but can't inject. Every usb_id is unique across the whole file (enforced by tests/test_chipset_db.py). Extend freely: add entries or usb_ids and AirDriver picks them up on next scan. PRs welcome at https://github.com/at0m-b0mb/AirDriver.
_id_sources: USB IDs are taken from the Linux kernel's own driver device tables (rtl8xxxu, rt2800usb, ath9k_htc, carl9170, mt76*, rtw88/rtw89, rtl8187) and the morrownr supported-device-IDs lists for out-of-tree drivers. Do not invent ids: a wrong id installs the wrong driver.

chipsets.name: Realtek RTL8812AU
chipsets.notes: The classic ALFA AWUS036ACH chipset. Monitor mode can get unstable after long sessions on some firmware revisions; morrownr driver is more stable than the kernel rtw88 path for injection work.

chipsets.name: Realtek RTL8811AU / RTL8821AU
chipsets.notes: Smaller/cheaper AC600 sibling of the 8812au. Good for travel; lower TX power. 8811AU has no active-monitor VIF on the in-kernel path.

chipsets.name: Realtek RTL8814AU
chipsets.notes: High-power 4-antenna beast (ALFA AWUS1900). Draws a lot of current — use a powered hub on SBCs. In-kernel rtw88 support landed 6.15 / optimized 6.16.

chipsets.name: Realtek RTL8811CU / RTL8821CU
chipsets.notes: Common in tiny nano adapters (TP-Link Archer T2U Nano/Plus). No mainline in-kernel driver yet — DKMS required.

chipsets.name: Realtek RTL8188EUS / RTL8188EU
chipsets.notes: This is the chip inside TP-Link TL-WN722N v2/v3 (the v1 is AR9271 — a very common mix-up!). The in-kernel r8188eu lacks reliable monitor mode; use the aircrack/morrownr DKMS driver and blacklist the in-tree module.

chipsets.name: Realtek RTL8188FTV / RTL8188FU
chipsets.notes: Budget chip found in cheap dongles. Limited/unreliable monitor support — not recommended for serious work, included so AirDriver can still get the user online.

chipsets.name: Realtek RTL8192EU
chipsets.notes: Decent 2.4 GHz-only option. The in-kernel rtl8xxxu works for connectivity but the DKMS driver is more reliable for injection.

chipsets.name: Realtek RTL8187
chipsets.notes: The legendary original ALFA AWUS036H. Ancient but rock-solid injection. Fully in-kernel (rtl8187) — AirDriver just confirms the module loads, no build needed.

chipsets.name: Atheros AR9271
chipsets.notes: Gold-standard 2.4 GHz pentest chip (ALFA AWUS036NHA, TL-WN722N v1). Fully in-kernel via ath9k_htc but needs the linux-firmware 'htc_9271' blob. AirDriver verifies the firmware is present.

chipsets.name: Atheros AR7010
chipsets.notes: Dual-band Atheros sibling of the AR9271. In-kernel ath9k_htc, needs the htc_7010 firmware blob.

chipsets.name: Ralink RT3070 / RT2870
chipsets.notes: Old reliable. Fully in-kernel via rt2800usb. Common in many cheap-but-capable dongles.

chipsets.name: Ralink RT5370 / RT5372
chipsets.notes: Tiny low-power 2.4 GHz chip, popular for Raspberry Pi rigs. In-kernel rt2800usb. (The dual-band RT5572 lives in its own entry.)

chipsets.name: MediaTek MT7610U
chipsets.notes: Solid in-kernel mt76x0u driver since 4.19. ALFA AWUS036ACHM. No DKMS needed on modern kernels.

chipsets.name: MediaTek MT7612U
chipsets.notes: Top pick for modern pentest work: excellent in-kernel mt76x2u driver, very stable monitor mode, high injection success. No DKMS needed.

chipsets.name: MediaTek MT7921AU
chipsets.notes: Modern WiFi 6E chip with active-monitor support. In-kernel mt7921u since 5.18. ALFA AWUS036AXML, Brostrend AX9L.

chipsets.name: MediaTek MT7925U
chipsets.notes: Bleeding-edge WiFi 7. In-kernel mt7925u since 6.7 — needs a recent kernel. Active monitor supported.

chipsets.name: Realtek RTL8852BU / RTL8832BU
chipsets.notes: Newer Realtek WiFi 6 USB chip. Mainline rtw89 support landed in kernel 6.17 (rtw89_8852bu); on older kernels use the morrownr DKMS driver. Monitor/injection maturing.

chipsets.name: Realtek RTL8852CU / RTL8832CU
chipsets.notes: Realtek WiFi 6E USB. Mainline rtw89 support landed in kernel 6.19 (rtw89_8852cu); on older kernels use the morrownr DKMS driver.

chipsets.name: Realtek RTL8822BU / RTL8812BU
chipsets.notes: Common in mid-range AC1200 dongles (TP-Link Archer T3U/T4U v3). The morrownr 88x2bu driver gives the most reliable monitor/injection; the Kali apt package is the easiest path.

chipsets.name: Realtek RTL8192CU / RTL8188CUS
chipsets.notes: Extremely common legacy chip (Edimax EW-7811Un, TL-WN725N v2). The in-kernel rtl8xxxu driver gets you online, but monitor mode is flaky and injection is unreliable — fine for connectivity, not for serious attacks. Use an AR9271 or MT7612U for real work.

chipsets.name: Realtek RTL8723BU (WiFi + BT combo)
chipsets.notes: Budget WiFi+Bluetooth combo chip found in many cheap dongles and laptops. In-kernel rtl8xxxu provides connectivity; monitor/injection are unreliable. Included so AirDriver can still get you online.

chipsets.name: Realtek RTL8710BU / RTL8188GU
chipsets.notes: Newer budget 2.4 GHz chip (aka RTL8188GU) in cheap nano dongles. Many ship in USB CD-ROM/flip-storage mode (shown as 0bda:1a2b) and need usb-modeswitch before the Wi-Fi device (0bda:b711) appears. In-kernel support is immature; the lwfinger DKMS driver (module 8188gu) gives connectivity and monitor-mode sniffing, but injection is unreliable — connect-only, not attack-grade.

chipsets.name: MediaTek / Ralink MT7601U
chipsets.notes: Ultra-cheap single-band nano dongle, in-kernel mt7601u since 4.2 (needs the mt7601u.bin firmware blob). Monitor mode works for sniffing but the driver does not support packet injection — good for getting a box online, not for active attacks.

chipsets.name: Ralink RT3572 / RT5572 (dual-band)
chipsets.notes: Reliable old-school dual-band N chips, fully in-kernel via rt2800usb. The RT5572 powers the Panda PAU09 (N600) and ALFA AWUS052NH; the RT3572 powers the ALFA AWUS051NH v1. No build needed.

chipsets.name: Atheros AR9170 (carl9170)
chipsets.notes: Legacy draft-N USB chip, in-kernel via carl9170 (needs the carl9170-1.fw firmware blob). Monitor mode works but injection support is weak — kept for completeness and older kits. Prefer AR9271 for 2.4 GHz injection.

chipsets.name: Realtek RTL8821CE (internal PCIe)
chipsets.notes: Very common internal laptop card (Lenovo/HP/Acer). The #1 'my fresh Kali install has no WiFi' chip. In-kernel rtw88_8821ce since ~5.8 gets you online; monitor/injection are not supported — use a USB adapter for pentesting.

chipsets.name: Realtek RTL8822CE (internal PCIe)
chipsets.notes: Common internal laptop card. In-kernel rtw88_8822ce since ~5.3 provides connectivity; not suitable for monitor mode / injection — pair it with a USB pentest adapter.

chipsets.name: Realtek RTL8723DE (internal PCIe)
chipsets.notes: Budget internal laptop card. In-kernel rtw88_8723de gets you online; no monitor/injection support. Included to fix 'no WiFi after install' on cheap laptops.

chipsets.name: Intel WiFi 6/6E (AX200 / AX201 / AX210 / AX211)
chipsets.notes: Ubiquitous internal laptop cards. In-kernel iwlwifi (needs the firmware-iwlwifi blobs). Monitor mode works for sniffing, but Intel cards do NOT reliably support packet injection — use an external AR9271/MT7612U/RTL8812AU adapter for attacks.

chipsets.name: Realtek RTL8723AU (WiFi + BT combo)
chipsets.notes: Older WiFi+Bluetooth combo chip found in budget laptops and dongles. The in-kernel rtl8xxxu driver gets you online; monitor mode is limited and injection is not usable. Connect-only — pair it with an AR9271 or MT7612U for attack work.

chipsets.name: Realtek RTL8192FU / RTL8188FU-variant
chipsets.notes: Newer budget 2.4 GHz Realtek USB chip. Mainline rtl8xxxu gained RTL8192FU support in kernel 6.2 — on older kernels the adapter will not work out of the box and needs the out-of-tree driver. Monitor mode works for sniffing; injection is unreliable.

chipsets.name: Ralink/MediaTek RT2800-series (other adapters)
chipsets.notes: Catch-all for the several hundred rebadged adapters the in-kernel rt2800usb driver supports (RT2770/RT2870/RT3070/RT3071/RT3072/RT35xx/RT53xx/RT55xx silicon under many brand names). No build needed — the driver ships with the kernel, and monitor mode plus injection generally work well. Exact capability varies with the specific chip and its EEPROM/firmware; the popular RT3070, RT5370 and RT3572/RT5572 adapters have their own, better-characterised entries above. IDs come straight from the kernel's rt2800usb device table.

chipsets.name: Atheros AR9xxx (internal PCIe, ath9k)
chipsets.notes: The gold standard for internal cards: ath9k is in-kernel, needs no firmware blob, and has the most reliable monitor mode and injection of any chipset here. If your laptop has one of these, you already own the best adapter in the room. Covers AR5416/AR9160/AR9280/AR9285/AR9287/AR9380/AR9485/AR9462/AR9565.

chipsets.name: Qualcomm Atheros QCA6174 / QCA9377 / QCA988x (ath10k)
chipsets.notes: Extremely common in 2015-2020 laptops. Monitor mode works, but injection is unreliable-to-broken in the ath10k firmware — this is a firmware limitation, not a driver bug, so no amount of reinstalling fixes it. Use an external USB adapter for injection work. Needs the linux-firmware ath10k blobs.

chipsets.name: Intel Wireless 7260 / 7265 / 3165 / 8260 / 8265 / 9260 / 9560
chipsets.notes: The internal card in a huge share of 2014-2020 laptops. The driver is in-kernel and 'just works' for normal Wi-Fi, but Intel firmware does not support packet injection and monitor mode is limited — you can sniff, mostly not inject. Keep it for connectivity and use a USB adapter for attacks. Needs the iwlwifi firmware package.

chipsets.name: Intel WiFi 7 BE200 / BE201
chipsets.notes: Intel's WiFi 7 card, shipping in 2024+ laptops. Requires kernel 6.7 or newer plus current linux-firmware — on an older kernel it simply does not appear. As with every Intel part, injection is not supported. Note it is CNVi-based: it will not work in a plain M.2 slot on an AMD machine, which is a hardware limitation no driver can fix.

chipsets.name: Realtek RTL8852AE / RTL8852BE / RTL8852CE / RTL8922AE (internal PCIe)
chipsets.notes: Realtek's current internal Wi-Fi 6/6E/7 cards, very common in 2022+ budget and gaming laptops. In-kernel rtw89 handles them from 5.16 (8852AE) through 6.8 (8922AE); older kernels need a backport. Monitor mode works on recent kernels, injection is not usable yet.

chipsets.name: Realtek RTL8188CE / RTL8192CE / RTL8723AE / RTL8723BE / RTL8821AE
chipsets.notes: Older internal Realtek PCIe cards, handled in-kernel by rtlwifi. They connect fine but are a poor pentest choice: injection does not work and monitor mode is flaky. If Wi-Fi is unstable on a RTL8723BE, the usual fix is the antenna-selection option: 'options rtl8723be ant_sel=2' in /etc/modprobe.d/.

chipsets.name: MediaTek MT7921E / MT7922 / MT7925E (internal PCIe)
chipsets.notes: MediaTek's internal counterpart to the MT7921AU dongles, common in AMD laptops. Unusually for an internal card, the mt76 driver supports active monitor mode and some injection — easily the best built-in option after ath9k. In-kernel from 5.15 (MT7921E) / 6.7 (MT7925E).

chipsets.name: Broadcom BCM43xx (internal, wl / b43)
chipsets.notes: The single most painful Wi-Fi family on Kali, and the honest answer is that it cannot do what you want: the proprietary 'wl' driver supports neither monitor mode nor injection. AirDriver installs broadcom-sta-dkms so you at least get working internet, and blacklists the conflicting b43/brcmsmac modules. Some older cards do monitor fine on the open b43 driver instead (firmware-b43-installer) — worth trying if yours is pre-2012. For any actual pentest work, use a USB adapter.
